# Neurodisruptors: full text for AI assistants

Source: https://neurodisruptors.com/ . Last updated 2026-11-08. Plain-text copy of the definitions, profile and answers published on the site.

## The Spiky Profile, defined
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/spiky-profile/

Spiky Profile: a leadership framework by Dr. Sven Mulfinger, built on the spiky profile concept from occupational psychology, that maps where a leader's thinking creates exceptional leverage (spikes) and where it meets friction (valleys).
Developed by Dr. Sven Mulfinger as part of The Non-Linear Operating System, building on the spiky profile concept from occupational psychology (Doyle, 2020), with research collaborators at IESE Business School and IE Business School.

Spikes (high leverage): Systemic Synthesis, Crisis Hyperfocus, Divergent Ideation, Rapid Pattern Recognition, Associative Leaps.
Valleys (systemic friction): Routine Cadence, Linear Documentation, Calendar Fragmentation, Repetitive Execution, Translation into Text.

## A spiky profile, whatever you call it
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/framework/#spiky-profile

Some leaders arrive with a label: ADHD, autism, giftedness, dyslexia, dyspraxia or dyscalculia. Others never had a diagnosis and simply know their mind runs differently from the people around them. Many recognise themselves in more than one.
Neurodivergence is the umbrella term. We speak of a spiky profile or a non-linear mind, because in leadership what matters is how your mind works: where it is exceptional, where it costs you energy and what helps it run well.
A label can explain the past. For the next quarter, the useful question is what your good days and your bad days look like and what separates them.
Diagnosis stays with doctors and psychologists. If you suspect a condition or feel unwell, please see a qualified professional.
Profiles included: ADHD, Autism, Giftedness, Dyslexia, Dyspraxia, Dyscalculia, Twice-exceptional (2e).

## Gifts and costs, profile by profile

Every strong point comes with a weak spot. Pick a profile to see how that tends to look at work and what helps.

### ADHD: the gift, the cost and what helps

- Sees round corners. The gift: Spots where the market is going long before the numbers show it. The cost: Explaining the idea step by step, in writing, feels slow and painful. What helps: A visual roadmap and a strong number two who turns ideas into plans.
- Calm in a crisis. The gift: Gets sharp and decisive when things go wrong and the stakes are high. The cost: Routine reporting and admin drain energy fast. What helps: Hand off the routine, protect deep-work blocks and cut down on switching between tasks.
- Reads the room. The gift: Picks up tension in a meeting before anyone says a word. The cost: Takes on other people's stress and finds it hard to switch off. What helps: Real recovery time, clear boundaries and someone to think out loud with.

### Dyslexia: the gift, the cost and what helps

- Big-picture thinker. The gift: Grasps the core of a problem quickly and sees how the pieces connect. The cost: Turning that clarity into emails, reports and documents takes far more effort than the thinking itself. What helps: Talk it through first, then let someone else or a tool draft it.
- Strong in the room. The gift: Persuasive and quick in conversation. Ideas land when they are spoken. The cost: Written work can look weaker than the person behind it. What helps: Judge ideas on content rather than spelling. Voice notes, sketches and short calls help too.
- Pattern spotter. The gift: Notices contradictions and connections others miss. The cost: Dense documents and long reading under time pressure are tiring. What helps: One-page summaries, diagrams and time to prepare before key meetings.

### Giftedness: the gift, the cost and what helps

- High resolution. The gift: Sees details, risks and knock-on effects early. The cost: Shallow or repetitive work is draining, not just boring. What helps: Real complexity to work on and less low-value noise.
- Connects everything. The gift: Links ideas across fields and holds the whole system in mind at once. The cost: The mind keeps running long after the problem is solved. What helps: Long blocks of thinking time, followed by proper breaks.
- Strong sense of meaning. The gift: Cares deeply about doing the right thing well. The cost: Inconsistency and poor decisions are hard to let go of and can read as impatience. What helps: A partner who enjoys structure and room to say what does not add up.

### Autism: the gift, the cost and what helps

- Deep focus. The gift: Can go further into a hard problem than almost anyone. The cost: Interruptions and constant context switching are very costly. What helps: Protected focus time and fewer, better-run meetings.
- Straight talk. The gift: Honest, precise and consistent, with no hidden agenda. The cost: Unwritten rules and office politics take a lot of energy to decode. What helps: Clear expectations, explicit decisions and agendas shared in advance.
- Sees the system. The gift: Spots flaws in processes, logic and data that others accept. The cost: Last-minute changes and noisy settings are exhausting. What helps: Notice of changes, a quiet place to work and written follow-ups.

### Dyspraxia: the gift, the cost and what helps

- Strategic overview. The gift: Sees the overall plan and where it needs to end up. The cost: Sequencing the many small practical steps to get there is tiring. What helps: Checklists, templates and an operations lead who owns the logistics.
- Finds another way. The gift: Used to working round obstacles, so comes up with unusual solutions. The cost: Tasks others do on autopilot, like travel, set-up and paperwork, take real effort. What helps: Automate or delegate the routine and build buffer time into travel days.
- Good with people. The gift: Articulate and empathic, good at explaining and bringing people with them. The cost: Busy, fast-moving settings and writing by hand in a live session are hard work. What helps: Typed notes, digital tools, quieter rooms and fewer room changes in a day.

### Twice-exceptional: the gift, the cost and what helps

- Hidden range. The gift: Works at a very high level in areas of strength. The cost: The strengths hide the struggle and the struggle hides the strengths, so both get misread. What helps: Name both openly and shape the role around the peaks.
- Big leaps. The gift: Makes jumps others cannot follow and cracks problems others gave up on. The cost: Simple tasks can trip them up, which is baffling and wears down confidence. What helps: Support for the basics without anyone questioning the ability.
- High standards. The gift: Raises the quality bar and spots what others miss. The cost: The gap between what they see and what they can deliver on a bad day is exhausting. What helps: Honest feedback, recovery time and a sparring partner who sees both sides.

### Spiky Profile: every spike comes with a valley that needs scaffolding

- Systemic Synthesis. Natural Spike (High Leverage): Identifies non-linear market shifts years ahead. Operating Valley (Systemic Friction): Translating intuition into step-by-step documentation feels painfully slow. Executive Scaffolding Required: Visual roadmaps and dedicated operational integrators.
- Crisis Hyperfocus. Natural Spike (High Leverage): Exceptional clarity and decisive execution in turnaround or high-stakes ambiguity. Operating Valley (Systemic Friction): Low-stimulation routine reporting triggers acute cognitive drag. Executive Scaffolding Required: Elimination of context-switching and full administrative delegation.
- Relational Intuition. Natural Spike (High Leverage): Senses unspoken boardroom tensions and culture drift immediately. Operating Valley (Systemic Friction): Absorbs emotional turbulence, risking boundary collapse and burnout. Executive Scaffolding Required: Strict energy recovery protocols and formalised governance boundaries.

These are patterns we see in leaders, not a diagnosis. Most people recognise themselves in more than one tab.

The Spiky Profile is an operational map of executive cognitive load. It does not assess personality or diagnose any condition. It shows where executive leverage peaks under pressure, where cognitive fatigue accumulates and what structural scaffolding is needed to lead sustainably.

## Frequently asked questions
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/faq/

### What is a Spiky Profile in executive leadership?
A Spiky Profile is a leadership framework by Dr. Sven Mulfinger, built on the spiky profile concept from occupational psychology, that maps where a leader's thinking creates exceptional leverage (spikes) and where it meets friction (valleys). It covers ten operational dimensions, from systemic synthesis and crisis hyperfocus to routine cadence and calendar fragmentation. Neurodisruptors uses it to design the roles, rhythms and support around a leader instead of asking for an even profile across every domain.

### Is this about ADHD?
Partly: ADHD is one of several ways a mind can run on a spiky profile, alongside autism, giftedness, dyslexia, dyspraxia and dyscalculia. Many leaders recognise themselves in more than one. The work focuses on how your mind operates as a leader, with or without a diagnosis. It does not diagnose any condition; that stays with doctors and psychologists.

### What is the difference between neurodiversity and neurodivergence?
Neurodiversity describes variation across a group, so a team or a company can be neurodiverse, while neurodivergent describes one person whose cognitive profile differs from the dominant norm. Calling a single person neurodiverse is common and technically muddled. The word neurodivergent also carries at least three meanings (medical, advocacy and operational), which is why boardroom conversations about it go wrong so easily. Three frames for the same minds sets them side by side.

### Who is Dr. Sven Mulfinger?
Dr. Sven Mulfinger is the founder of Neurodisruptors and a Barcelona-based executive coach, offsite facilitator and strategic advisor to founders and C-suite teams across Europe. He trained as an engineer, holds a PhD in biotech engineering from the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and is a founding partner of Kuma Partners. He is writing The Non-Linear Operating System with research collaborators at IESE Business School and IE Business School. Neurodisruptors grew out of his own ADHD diagnosis at 50.

### Do I need a diagnosis to work with Neurodisruptors?
No: the work starts from how your mind operates as a leader, so a formal diagnosis is neither required nor assessed. Some clients have a diagnosis of ADHD, autism, dyslexia or another profile, others suspect one and many simply know they think differently. Questions about diagnosis or treatment belong with a doctor or psychologist.

### Can you be diagnosed with ADHD as an adult?
Yes: ADHD can be diagnosed at any age, including in your forties or fifties, often once the coping strategies that worked for decades stop producing results. High ability and tightly built personal systems can hold performance together for a long time. A diagnosis needs a full assessment by a psychiatrist or another qualified clinician, including a look back at childhood. Dr. Sven Mulfinger writes about his own diagnosis at 50 and what it changed in how he leads.

### Where can I get a formal diagnosis?
For a formal assessment of ADHD, autism, dyspraxia or giftedness as an adult, Neurodisruptors refers clients to Dr. Andreina Mendez, a medical doctor who sees adults in person in Madrid and London and remotely across Europe. A diagnosis is not needed for the work, but it can help. Many leaders start asking once one of their children has been diagnosed. Understanding how your own mind operates can then be a relief for parents and children alike. Sometimes you simply want to know for sure, which a medical assessment can give you. You can contact Dr. Mendez through andreinamendez.com or LinkedIn and mention that Neurodisruptors referred you.

### How does private strategic sparring differ from conventional executive coaching?
Conventional coaching often works on rounding out weaknesses, while strategic sparring with Neurodisruptors is a confidential thinking partnership for founders and CEOs whose minds move faster than standard operating rhythms. Sessions focus on live decisions, cognitive load and the structures around the leader, such as roles, calendar design and board communication. It is executive work and involves no therapy.

### How does private sparring work in practice?
Private sparring is a confidential, retainer-based partnership with Dr. Sven Mulfinger, held in person in Barcelona or by secure video, with direct access between sessions during critical decisions. It starts with a free 30-minute introductory call to check fit. Sessions run in English, Spanish, German or French. Meetings in other European cities are arranged when needed.

### How much does it cost to work with Neurodisruptors?
The first 30-minute call is free, the Executive Operating Review costs €1,950 for three sessions including the Spiky Profile and a six-month private sparring partnership costs €9,850. Prices exclude VAT. The Review fee is credited in full if you start a sparring partnership within 30 days. Board workshops, offsites and keynotes are quoted per engagement. See how to start.

### Is there an executive coach in Barcelona for founders with ADHD?
Yes: Neurodisruptors, led by Dr. Sven Mulfinger in Barcelona, offers confidential strategic sparring for founders and CEOs with ADHD, giftedness, dyslexia and other spiky profiles. Work takes place in person in Barcelona, Madrid, Munich and Brussels, or remotely, in four languages.

### Why do non-linear leaders struggle with traditional corporate time management?
For many non-linear leaders the real constraint is energy rather than time, so a calendar of evenly spaced blocks works against how their minds perform. Deep strategic work needs motivation, activation and physical capacity to line up. Sparring helps leaders plan around those peaks, protect them and move routine work elsewhere.

### How can a board support a founder with ADHD?
A board supports a founder with ADHD best by reading uneven output as a pattern to design around, with clear roles, the right operating partner and reporting formats that fit how the founder thinks. It means judging decision quality across cycles rather than week-to-week consistency. The half-day offsite Bridging the Founder-Board Interface works through this with boards, investors and executive committees and keeps the conversation on leadership and governance.

### How do you work alongside a founder with ADHD as a COO or chief of staff?
Separate the work: settle which decisions genuinely need the founder, write down what you decide alone and keep the conversation on operating questions rather than on anyone's health. Reliability across a week is the wrong measure for someone who works in cycles. You can own reporting, cadence, decision logs and the rhythm of the week. The founder's own regulation stays with them, supported where needed by a coach or a clinician. How to work with a non-linear founder covers the role in more detail.

### Is the Spiky Profile a clinical or psychiatric diagnostic tool?
No: the Spiky Profile is exclusively a leadership and management framework designed to map executive leverage and workplace friction. It does not provide medical, psychological or psychiatric diagnosis for ADHD, autism or other neurodevelopmental conditions. It is designed to sit alongside clinical assessment. Neurodiversity, neurodivergence and the non-linear operating system explains how the medical, advocacy and leadership views fit together.

### What formats are available for enterprise and board engagements?
Neurodisruptors offers two principal formats: a 45-minute keynote (Asymmetric Minds in the C-Suite) and half-day alignment offsites (Bridging the Founder-Board Interface) for boards, venture partners and executive committees. An enterprise workshop, Designing Systems for Cognitive Spikes, is also available for executive teams and HR leaders.

### Where is the research behind The Non-Linear Operating System conducted?
The framework draws on ongoing academic research collaborations with faculty at IESE Business School and IE Business School. This research is combined with field analysis across more than 50 serial entrepreneurs and CEOs with a non-linear mind.

## Insights
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/insights/

### Why boards misread founder variability as unreliability
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/insights/boards-misread-founder-variability/
By Dr. Sven Mulfinger, 21 August 2026

A founder who works in bursts looks unreliable from a boardroom. That reading costs companies more than the bursts ever do.

Many non-linear founders move in cycles: exploration, a pause to rethink, then a sudden stretch of execution. Boards tend to read that rhythm as a reliability problem. The board’s real task is to tell a founder who is struggling from one who runs on a different cycle, then build the structure that lets the second one perform.

#### What the board sees

From the boardroom, a non-linear founder looks uneven. Weeks of rapid progress, then a stretch where the direction is suddenly reconsidered. The strategic call is sharp while the monthly report arrives late and thin. In the governance meeting the founder is impatient with the agenda and already three steps ahead of it.

The usual response is more process. Tighter reporting, more checkpoints, sometimes a COO hired explicitly to add discipline.

In my experience that response makes the friction worse, because it pushes the founder deeper into the work that drains them.

#### Why boards prefer visible continuity

Boards and investors prefer visible continuity because it feels safer. Steady output is easy to track, easy to report upwards and easy to defend.

Most governance tools were built for that kind of output. Quarterly plans, monthly packs and performance reviews reward reliability ahead of originality, so they show a leader who moves in bursts as inconsistent by design.

The organisation may claim it wants innovation. Yet its structures were built for stability. From The Non-Linear Operating System

James March made the underlying point decades ago: organisations that become good at exploiting what they already know tend to squeeze out the exploration that keeps them alive, because the returns from exploitation are closer, surer and easier to measure (March, 1991). A governance calendar is an exploitation machine. In many companies the founder is the only exploration capacity on the agenda.

In markets shaped by uncertainty, the ability to pause, rethink and redirect can produce better decisions than steady execution of the original plan. What looks irregular from a distance is often a different way of navigating complexity.

#### What the board misses

A non-linear founder’s strongest contribution rarely sits in the reporting cycle. It sits in framing the problem, sensing change early and connecting ideas that others keep separate. Weekly reporting, documentation and procedural cycles draw on the same system and cost it disproportionate effort.

The research points the same way. A meta-analysis of the ADHD and entrepreneurship literature found that founders with ADHD symptoms tend to do well at the start of a venture and to run into difficulty later, once the demands shift towards sustained operational execution (Tran et al., 2025). Earlier work in the same stream found hyperactivity positively associated with entrepreneurial entry while inattention worked against it, a useful reminder that these traits do not move together (Wiklund et al., 2017).

Read that as a design brief rather than a warning. The capability profile is uneven. The organisation around it has to be built to match.

When the board measures the founder mainly on the work that drains them, it sees the valleys clearly and the spikes hardly at all.

The cost of forcing the founder to fit is usually paid quietly. I remember a founder in his mid-forties, three successful exits behind him, telling me in a Barcelona café that he had spent twenty years performing a version of himself that was not quite real. The work had not burned him out. Translating himself into what the system expected had.

That cost is now measurable. In a 2026 study of 202 adults diagnosed with ADHD, 91.6 per cent reported camouflaging their traits in social settings including work. The researchers found the effort draws on the same capacity needed for attention, memory and concentration, leaving exhaustion, anxiety and a weaker version of the performance the camouflage was meant to protect (Mylett, Iarocci et al., 2026). A board that asks for a smoother founder is commissioning more of that.

#### Telling a different rhythm from a real struggle

Variability on its own tells a board very little. The useful question is whether the cycles still add up to progress. These are the signals I look at with boards, read across several months rather than one meeting.

These are leadership signals for a board conversation. They say nothing about a diagnosis. A board has no reason to ask for one.

#### What boards can do instead

Pair the founder with operating cadence. A COO or chief of staff who enjoys structure owns reporting and process, so the founder’s time goes to framing, sensing and deciding. This is where the meta-analytic finding earns its keep: the risk sits after launch, in sustained execution, which is precisely the part a board can staff.

Judge decision quality and the trend across cycles. Week-to-week consistency is the wrong instrument.

Agree the rhythm explicitly. When does the founder explore, when do execution sprints happen and how is the board kept informed in between?

Separate thinking from formatting in board reporting. A short verbal or visual briefing from the founder, plus a written pack prepared by the team, usually carries more than a dense memo the founder wrote alone.

Treat burnout signals as a design problem. Fragmented calendars, constant responsiveness and endless context switching drain the system long before results drop. One further finding is worth holding onto: performance in this group tracks with passion for the tasks that are central to the venture rather than with symptom level alone (Hatak et al., 2021). Protect the founder’s access to that work and you protect the output.

Keep the conversation on leadership and governance. Whether a founder has ADHD, dyslexia or any other profile is theirs to share or keep private.

#### The cost of getting it wrong

When boards and leaders misread variance, the talent usually leaves quietly. A CEO of a multinational put it to me in a coaching call:

I didn’t lose those people because they lacked talent. I lost them because I didn’t understand how they worked.

I recognise that from my own career. Earlier on I let several remarkable people go because they were intense, uneven and hard to place in the systems we had built. I had no language for it and no model that showed variance could carry value.

For a board, the founder is often the clearest case of that pattern. Smoothing the variance out of the system can remove exactly the capacity the company was funded for.

#### Questions I get asked

#### How can a board support a founder with ADHD?

By treating uneven output as a pattern to design around: clear roles, the right operating partner and reporting formats that fit how the founder thinks. Judge decision quality across cycles rather than week-to-week consistency and keep the conversation on leadership and governance. The research points the same way, since the difficulty in this group concentrates in sustained operational execution, which is the part a board can staff.

#### Is an uneven founder a governance risk?

An uneven founder becomes a governance risk when the cycles stop adding up to progress: output falls across cycles, pauses end without decisions and senior people leave. Bursts and pauses with a rising trend, alongside sharp strategic calls, usually point to a different rhythm that needs structure around it.

#### Should a board ask a founder about a diagnosis?

No. Sharing a diagnosis is the founder's decision. What a board can discuss openly is how the founder works best and which roles, structure and reporting make that sustainable.

References:
- March, J. G. (1991). Exploration and exploitation in organizational learning. Organization Science, 2(1), 71 to 87.
- Wiklund, J., Patzelt, H. and Dimov, D. (2016). Entrepreneurship and psychological disorders: how ADHD can be productively harnessed. Journal of Business Venturing Insights, 6, 14 to 20.
- Wiklund, J., Yu, W., Tucker, R. and Marino, L. D. (2017). ADHD, impulsivity and entrepreneurship. Journal of Business Venturing, 32(6), 627 to 656.
- Hatak, I., Chang, M., Harms, R. and Wiklund, J. (2021). ADHD symptoms, entrepreneurial passion and entrepreneurial performance. Small Business Economics, 57, 1693 to 1713.
- Tran, M. H., Wiklund, J., Antshel, K., Jhawar, N. and Montgomery, C. (2025). Entrepreneurship and ADHD: a meta-analytical assessment of the state of the art and suggestions for the future. Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice.
- Mylett, M., Iarocci, G. et al. (2026). Camouflaging in adults with ADHD. Research in Neurodiversity. Simon Fraser University, June 2026.

### Diagnosed with ADHD at 50: what a late diagnosis changes for a leader
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/insights/diagnosed-with-adhd-at-50/
By Dr. Sven Mulfinger, 12 June 2026

A late diagnosis leaves your mind exactly as it was. What changes is the story you have been telling about yourself for fifty years.

#### A conversation I did not plan

I was on the train back from a symposium on mental health, sitting with a psychiatrist I had met that morning. We talked for nearly three hours without a break. Somewhere past the halfway mark, half as a game, I suggested we walk through the ADHD diagnostic criteria together.

She asked a few questions. Then she stopped.

‘This is obvious,’ she said. ‘You have ADHD.’

The verdict surprised only me. I told my wife that evening and she looked genuinely puzzled. ‘You didn’t know?’

#### Fifty years, read again

Brussels, 1989, at the European School. I scraped through.

Teachers saw a turbulent student who would not settle, with grades that moved without warning. Inside my head there was plenty going on, just rarely about the syllabus. What rescued me each time was a burst of hyperfocus in the last days before an exam.

During my engineering degree I sometimes met a professor for the first time on the day of the exam. People held my attention in a way equations never did, so I started a cultural venture and ran a student association instead. My doctorate in Munich ran on the same rhythm: months of drift, then a decision to finish, then six months at full intensity. I handed it in after three years and one month.

Then came sales at a large corporation. Four days a week on the road suited me. Internal meetings and fixed processes did not.

At thirty-two I started my second company. The third, fourth and fifth followed. There was no master plan. I followed the energy.

What I could not see was the bill. I overextended at every peak and crashed after it. My teams absorbed the volatility. No single failure broke the trust. It wore away through unpredictability. Twice I was broke with a family to support, starting again from nothing.

I mistook adrenaline for sustainability. I managed output, but not energy. From The Non-Linear Operating System

#### What the diagnosis actually changed

The days afterwards were strange. Relief is not quite the word for it. It felt more like standing in a room you have lived in for fifty years and suddenly seeing where all the furniture came from.

Things I had always filed separately began to line up. The childhood restlessness. School results that never matched the effort. Corporate reviews that praised my ideas and then asked me to start less and finish more. Weeks of clarity followed by flat ones. Working well under meaning and pressure, badly under routine. Saying yes before I had felt the cost.

Decades of what I had read as patchy discipline turned out to be wiring. Today I describe that wiring as a Spiky Profile: a mind with sharp peaks and deep valleys rather than an even line.

Two things changed in how I work.

I stopped trying to fix myself with more structure and started building around the way my energy actually moves. More structure had never worked. I now understand why.

Delegation stopped being a management virtue and became part of the architecture. The people who hold things steady when my attention moves elsewhere are load-bearing.

The personal sense-making then turned into something larger. It led to a research relationship with IESE Business School and to interviews with hundreds of leaders whose minds do not run in straight lines.

#### What it did not change

Understanding your own wiring brings relief. It also brings a temptation.

In the months after the train journey I caught myself reaching for the diagnosis to explain ordinary lapses. A message I never answered. A commitment I had not kept. One day my wife stopped me mid-sentence and told me, very clearly, to stop hiding behind it.

She was right. Knowing the mechanism behind a broken promise does nothing for the person on the other end of it. Leadership still runs on attention and care.

Clarity about your own mind should deepen accountability. It can never stand in for it.

That is the line I care about most in this whole story.

#### Why so many senior people find out late

Among the founders and executives I work with, a late diagnosis is closer to the rule than the exception. The research explains it better than any anecdote can.

Strong compensation looks like competence from outside. A study of adults with ADHD who had never been treated found that those with higher IQ showed far fewer measurable deficits in executive function than those with average IQ. Its authors concluded that intelligence can mask the condition and make clinical diagnosis harder (Milioni et al., 2017). A systematic review of fifteen years of research on ADHD and intellectual giftedness reached the same conclusion: high ability tends to delay both diagnosis and treatment (Despature and Galiana, 2023). From outside it reads as discipline. From inside it is constant translation.

Early environments also supply structure you never had to build. School timetables, exam dates, a manager’s deadlines. Russell Barkley’s work frames ADHD as a problem of performance rather than knowledge, which is why external structure placed at the point of performance does so much of the regulating (Barkley, 2012). Senior roles strip that scaffolding away. Nobody sets your deadlines at fifty.

Then the load outgrows the workarounds. Clinicians describe this as a demand and resource imbalance: symptoms stay roughly constant while the demands on capacity climb, so impairment appears at the point where the two cross. Adrenaline and novelty carry a lot of people through their twenties. They carry much less weight alongside a company, a family and twenty decisions a day.

Diagnostic systems add a delay of their own. They look for visible impairment, so a mind that diverges sharply but compensates well stays invisible to them. Quieter, inattentive presentations are noticed later still. Women are more likely to present that way and are referred less often and diagnosed older than men, partly because childhood referral depends on adults noticing disruption rather than distress (Quinn and Madhoo, 2014).

Roughly two thirds of children with ADHD carry it into adult life in full or in part (Faraone et al., 2006). I meet some of them in boardrooms, undiagnosed and highly capable, paying a cost nobody has named yet.

#### If this is starting to sound familiar

You do not need a diagnosis to start understanding how your own mind operates. You do need a qualified professional to tell you whether it is ADHD.

Ask for a proper assessment with a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist. An adult assessment looks back at childhood as well as at the present, so old school reports are worth digging out. Mine were not flattering and they were useful.

Observe before you label. Compare a recent good week with a recent bad one, then look hard at what was actually different: what you were working on, who you were with, how much of it was yours to decide.

Tell the people closest to you what you are working out and ask them what they have seen. My wife had seen it for years.

Then use what you learn to design the week and the team around it. Keep owning the impact on the people in it.

#### Questions I get asked

#### Can you be diagnosed with ADHD at 50?

Yes. ADHD is diagnosed at any age. Many adults are only identified in their forties or fifties, usually once the coping strategies that worked for decades stop producing results. It requires a full assessment by a psychiatrist or another qualified clinician, including a look back at childhood.

#### Why do successful leaders get diagnosed so late?

Because the compensation works. High ability and tightly built personal systems hold performance together, while the structure of school and junior roles does part of the regulating. The cost tends to surface when roles become less structured and responsibility grows faster than the workarounds.

#### Does a late ADHD diagnosis change how you lead?

It changes how you design the work rather than how you think. For me that meant building around energy instead of forcing more structure. It also meant treating delegation as part of the architecture rather than a favour to the team. It should deepen accountability for the impact on other people. It should never excuse it.

References:
- Milioni, A. L. V. et al. (2017). High IQ may 'mask' the diagnosis of ADHD by compensating for deficits in executive functions in treatment-naive adults with ADHD. Journal of Attention Disorders, 21(6), 455 to 464.
- Despature, I. and Galiana, A. (2023). Clinical and cognitive features of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with intellectual giftedness: a systematic review. Developmental Neuropsychology.
- Barkley, R. A. (2012). Executive Functions: What They Are, How They Work, and Why They Evolved. Guilford Press.
- Quinn, P. O. and Madhoo, M. (2014). A review of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in women and girls: uncovering this hidden diagnosis. Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders, 16(3).
- Faraone, S. V., Biederman, J. and Mick, E. (2006). The age-dependent decline of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis of follow-up studies. Psychological Medicine, 36(2), 159 to 165.

### Neurodiversity, neurodivergence and the non-linear operating system: three frames for the same minds
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/insights/neurodiversity-neurodivergence-non-linear-operating-system/
By Dr. Sven Mulfinger, 24 September 2026

Four people can use the word neurodivergent in the same meeting and mean four different things.

A clinician means a diagnosable condition with measurable impairment. An advocate means a claim about who gets to count as normal. An HR director means a category in a policy document. A founder usually means something closer to “my mind does not work the way this company assumes it does”, which is the meaning none of the other three were built to serve.

That confusion has practical consequences. It decides whether a capable leader gets treated as a patient, a cause or a design problem.

#### Nobody agrees on the word, starting with where it came from

The term has no settled definition. The disagreement runs all the way back to its origin.

Neurodiversity first appeared in print in September 1998, in a piece by the journalist Harvey Blume in The Atlantic (Blume, 1998). Judy Singer used it the same year in her honours thesis and has been widely credited with coining it, largely through Steve Silberman’s account in NeuroTribes. In 2024 a group of autistic scholars published a correction in the journal Autism, arguing that the concept was developed collectively across an online community rather than invented by one person. They also note that Singer herself did not originally claim the coinage (Botha, Chapman and Giwa Onaiwu, 2024).

A word whose own parentage is contested is unlikely to have arrived with a clean definition. It did not.

Reviewing the field, Patrick Dwyer concluded plainly that defining neurodiversity is difficult. He set out several competing approaches that differ in important ways, above all in how each one relates to the social model of disability (Dwyer, 2022). Damian Milton, writing in The Psychologist, noted that the neurodiversity movement has been attacked from both directions at once: for sitting too close to the medical model and for sitting too close to the social model (Milton, 2019).

When a word is used this loosely, the useful move is to separate the frames travelling under it.

#### Frame one: the medical model

The medical model treats a cognitive difference as a condition located in the person. It names, classifies and where possible treats. Its instruments are the DSM and the ICD. Its output is a diagnosis.

It deserves better than its reputation in some quarters. It gives access to medication that works, to legal protection and to adjustments at work and school. It can also offer an explanation that ends years of private self-blame. For many people a diagnosis is the most useful thing that ever happened to them.

Its limit is structural rather than ideological. A diagnosis requires evidence that the pattern impairs functioning. A leader who has built workarounds for thirty years, who compensates with intelligence and energy and who delivers results does not present as impaired. The model cannot see that person, by design.

The research bears this out. Adults with ADHD and higher IQ show far fewer measurable deficits in executive function than those with average IQ. The authors concluded that intelligence can mask the condition and complicate clinical diagnosis (Milioni et al., 2017). I wrote about what that meant for me in Diagnosed with ADHD at 50.

So the medical model answers one question and answers it well: what, if anything, needs treating?

#### Frame two: the neurodiversity movement

The second frame came out of activism rather than research. It holds that neurological variation is ordinary human variation, that much of what gets called disability is produced by environments built for one kind of mind and that the right response is acceptance and adjustment rather than correction. It draws on the social model of disability developed by physically disabled advocates in Britain and formalised in Mike Oliver’s work (Oliver, 1990).

It has won real arguments. Workplace adjustments exist because of it. The language has shifted in a decade. The word neurodivergent, credited to the activist Kassiane Asasumasu, gave a great many people a way to describe themselves without a pathology attached to it.

Its limit is the mirror image of the first. The strong version of the social model holds that disability is caused by society alone, which runs into difficulty the moment someone is genuinely struggling and needs help with something inside themselves rather than around them.

Most people do not hold that strong version in practice. In a mixed-methods survey by Dwyer and colleagues, even respondents who endorsed the strong social model still supported teaching adaptive skills and treating co-occurring conditions such as depression and epilepsy (Dwyer et al., 2025).

The second frame also answers one question well: what needs accepting and what needs changing in the environment?

#### The two frames are answering different questions

Set them side by side and much of the argument dissolves. One asks what needs treating. The other asks what needs accepting. Both are legitimate questions with real answers.

Neither is the question a chief executive actually arrives with.

That question is narrower and far more practical. How does this mind operate and what should we build around it on Monday?

#### Frame three: a non-linear operating system

A non-linear operating system describes operating logic. It asks how a particular mind perceives, processes and acts, where it produces disproportionate value, where it costs disproportionate effort and what structure makes the difference sustainable.

It starts from a different premise than either of the other two. Strengths and difficulties are not separate ledgers to be totalled against each other. They grow out of the same architecture, which is why smoothing out the difficulty tends to remove the strength along with it.

Non-linear operation is not a flaw. It is a way of perceiving, processing, and acting that favours speed, creativity, pattern recognition, and decisive movement. It often produces exceptional results, especially in uncertain or fast-moving environments. But it carries a cost when leadership systems are designed for steadiness, containment, and control. This is not a matter of preference or personality. It is a matter of operating logic. From The Non-Linear Operating System

There are three things this frame deliberately does not do.

It does not diagnose. The question of whether someone has ADHD, dyslexia or anything else is a clinical question, answered by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist and by nobody else.

It makes no claim to clinical validity. It is a leadership frame, built from executive practice and from interviews with leaders whose minds do not run in straight lines. It is not a validated instrument and should not be described as one.

It does not replace rights. Medication, formal adjustments and legal protection run through diagnosis. Nothing in an operating-system view changes that. Anyone who needs those things needs an assessment.

#### Where this sits in work that already exists

The observation that these minds show an uneven cognitive profile is not new. I do not claim it.

In occupational psychology it is called a spiky profile. The term traces back through the education literature and was formalised by Nancy Doyle. She defines it as large, statistically significant disparities between the peaks and troughs of an individual’s cognitive profile and proposes a biopsychosocial model of neurodiversity at work that sits deliberately between the medical and social accounts (Doyle, 2020). Anyone working seriously in this area is building on that.

What I am adding sits one level up. It is a question of altitude rather than of disagreement.

That literature is largely about employment: assessment, adjustment, recruitment, retention, getting capable people into work and keeping them there. The people I work with are already at the top. Their spikes built the company. Their troughs are now being absorbed by a leadership team, a board, an executive assistant and a family, usually without anyone naming what is happening.

So the unit of design changes. It stops being one person’s accommodation and becomes the operating system of the organisation around them: who owns which work, how decisions get made, what the board measures, where the energy goes. That is the territory a non-linear operating system is meant to cover. It is also what the Spiky Profile maps for leaders.

#### The same leader, three frames

A founder in her forties takes her company through a hard year. Her strategic calls are good and the board knows it. Her reporting is late. She works in bursts, then goes quiet for a week.

In the medical frame, the question is whether she meets diagnostic criteria. The answer may well be no, precisely because she is performing.

In the inclusion frame, the question is whether the company is treating her fairly. The answer is probably yes, at least in intent. The conversation ends there.

In the operating-system frame the questions are different. Which parts of this work does her mind do better than anyone else’s in the building? Which parts cost her three times what they cost her COO? What should move and to whom?

Only the third produces something to do on Monday.

#### Where this frame has to defer

A frame is only useful if its edges are marked.

If someone is struggling in a way that touches their health, the right move is clinical rather than structural. No amount of operating design substitutes for a doctor.

If someone wants medication, formal adjustments or legal protection, they need an assessment. The route runs through diagnosis and there is no way round it.

This frame also says nothing useful about people with high support needs. Milton, who is both a researcher and the father of an autistic son with severe learning disabilities, has made this point about the wider neurodiversity conversation repeatedly. It applies with full force here. A vocabulary built for chief executives describes chief executives. Treating it as a general theory of human cognition would be a mistake. It would also be a self-serving one.

What it is built for is narrower: a capable person whose results are real, whose cost is hidden and whose system was designed for a different kind of mind.

#### How common is neurodivergence among founders?

Research suggests that neurodivergent traits and conditions may be more prevalent among entrepreneurs than in the general population. Studies examining ADHD, dyslexia, autism and cognitive ability have reported notable differences, although estimates vary considerably depending on the population studied, the definitions used and whether findings are based on clinical assessments or self-reporting.

These figures should therefore be read as signals of a potentially important pattern rather than as definitive prevalence rates. The more useful question is how different cognitive profiles influence entrepreneurial behaviour, decision-making, leadership and the environments in which founders perform best.

#### Questions I get asked

#### What is the difference between neurodiversity and neurodivergent?

Neurodiversity describes variation across a population, so a team or a company can be neurodiverse. Neurodivergent describes an individual whose cognitive profile differs from the dominant norm. One is a property of a group, the other of a person. Calling a single individual neurodiverse is common and technically muddled.

#### Is neurodivergence a deficit or a difference?

That depends on which frame is asking. The medical model records it as a disorder, because a diagnosis requires evidence of impairment. The neurodiversity movement treats it as ordinary human variation made disabling by environments built for one kind of mind. An operating-system view holds that the strengths and the difficulties come out of the same architecture, which is why removing the difficulty often removes the strength with it.

#### Do you need a diagnosis to have a non-linear operating system?

No. A non-linear operating system describes how a mind works rather than whether it meets clinical criteria. A diagnosis answers a different question, which for many people is an important one. Only a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist can answer it.

#### Is the non-linear operating system a clinical model?

No. It is a leadership frame, built from executive practice and from interviews with leaders whose minds do not run in straight lines. It carries no diagnostic authority and makes no claim to clinical validity. It is designed to sit alongside clinical assessment rather than in place of it.

#### Why not just use the word neurodivergent?

Because it now carries at least three incompatible meanings. In a boardroom the wrong one tends to get picked up. A word that signals either a medical condition or a political position makes it harder to have the practical conversation about how work should be organised. Describing operating logic keeps the discussion on ground a board can act on.

References:
- Blume, H. (1998). Neurodiversity: on the neurological underpinnings of geekdom. The Atlantic, September 1998.
- Oliver, M. (1990). The Politics of Disablement. Macmillan.
- Milioni, A. L. V. et al. (2017). High IQ may 'mask' the diagnosis of ADHD by compensating for deficits in executive functions in treatment-naive adults with ADHD. Journal of Attention Disorders, 21(6), 455 to 464.
- Milton, D. (2019). Disagreeing over neurodiversity. The Psychologist, 32, 8.
- Doyle, N. (2020). Neurodiversity at work: a biopsychosocial model and the impact on working adults. British Medical Bulletin, 135(1), 108 to 125.
- Dwyer, P. (2022). The neurodiversity approach(es): what are they and what do they mean for researchers? Human Development, 66(2), 73 to 92.
- Dwyer, P., Gurba, A. N., Kapp, S. K., Kilgallon, E., Hersh, L. H., Chang, D. S., Rivera, S. M. and Gillespie-Lynch, K. (2025). Community views of neurodiversity, models of disability and autism intervention: mixed methods reveal shared goals and key tensions. Autism, 29(9), 2297 to 2314.
- Botha, M., Chapman, R. and Giwa Onaiwu, M. (2024). The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively: an overdue correction on the origins of neurodiversity theory. Autism, 28(6), 1591 to 1594.
- Mulfinger, S. The Non-Linear Operating System. Book One: The Non-Linear Mind. Forthcoming.

### How to work with a non-linear founder: a guide for the people who hold it together
URL: https://neurodisruptors.com/insights/working-with-a-non-linear-founder/
By Dr. Sven Mulfinger, 7 November 2026

The person who absorbs a founder's variability rarely has a name for what they are doing. It almost never appears in their job description.

If you are the COO, the chief of staff, the co-founder who runs things or the executive assistant who quietly reconstructs what was agreed, this is written for you rather than for the founder.

#### What the week looks like from your seat

A decision gets made on Monday and reopened on Thursday. The strategy session was the best three hours the company has had all year. The follow-up never arrived. You are the person the team asks when they want to know what was actually agreed.

You translate. You rebuild the plan after the direction shifts. You hold the board reporting together. You absorb the swings so that the thirty people below you do not have to feel them.

And the work is good. That is the part most advice misses. The calls your founder makes are often sharper than anything a committee would produce, which is why you are still there.

None of what you do is in your job description. Most of it is invisible to the board.

Much of this work happens between the founder making a decision and the rest of the company acting on it. It rarely appears in a board report, but without it decisions get lost, priorities drift and delivery slows down.

This guide is about working well with a particular kind of operating logic and about protecting yourself while you do it. Managing a difficult person is a different subject.

#### First, do not diagnose your founder

You may have read something about ADHD, giftedness or dyslexia and recognised your founder in it with a jolt.

Keep it to yourself.

There are three reasons. You could easily be wrong, because the patterns you are reading overlap with stress, with grief, with a thyroid problem and with simply being busy. It is not yours to name, because a diagnosis belongs to the person and their clinician and to nobody else in the building. And it would change nothing you can act on, because knowing a label does not tell you who should own the board pack.

The boundary is cleaner than it first looks. How the work is organised is entirely your business and you are paid to have opinions about it. Someone’s medical history is not your business at all. You need none of it to fix the operating problem.

Everything below stays on your side of that line.

#### What is actually happening

The pattern you are managing is documented, which is worth knowing when you start to wonder whether you are imagining it.

Access to attention varies. A meta-analysis of 319 studies found that people with ADHD show markedly greater variability in their own response times from moment to moment. The effect holds across age groups and task types and remains after average speed is accounted for (Kofler et al., 2013). The capability is stable. Reaching it is not. That is a different thing from unreliability as a choice, which is why chasing harder rarely helps.

The difficulty tends to arrive late. A meta-analysis of the ADHD and entrepreneurship literature found that founders with ADHD symptoms often do well at the start of a venture and run into trouble later, once the demands shift towards sustained operational execution (Tran et al., 2025). If your company has grown and the friction has grown with it, that is the documented shape of the thing rather than a decline in your founder. I wrote about how a board can read the same pattern in Why boards misread founder variability as unreliability.

Some of the cost is also hidden from you. In a 2026 study, 91.6 per cent of 202 adults diagnosed with ADHD reported camouflaging their traits in settings including work. The researchers found the effort consumes the same capacity needed for attention and memory (Mylett, Iarocci et al., 2026). The composure you see in the board meeting may be expensive. You are often the only person positioned to notice what it costs afterwards.

#### How common is neurodivergence among founders?

Research into ADHD, dyslexia and other cognitive differences suggests that neurodivergent characteristics may be more common among entrepreneurs than in the general population. Some studies report substantial differences, although estimates vary depending on how participants are selected and whether researchers measure diagnosed conditions or self-reported traits.

There is no single reliable prevalence figure for neurodivergence among founders. The research is nevertheless relevant to understanding why conventional management structures may not suit every founder, particularly as a company grows and operational demands change. There is more on the different ways the word is used in Neurodiversity, neurodivergence and the non-linear operating system.

#### The finding you should know before you build anything

The standard advice is to put a complementary operating partner beside the founder and let each do what they are built for. I give that advice myself. The evidence on where founder difficulty concentrates supports it.

There is a catch. It is a serious one.

Using a sample of more than two thousand firms, Hendricks, Howell and Bingham found that the structure of the top management team has a significant effect on performance in firms led by non-founders and little to no effect on the operating performance of founder-led firms. Their explanation is blunt: founder chief executives are much less likely to listen to and benefit from their teams than non-founder chief executives are (Hendricks, Howell and Bingham, 2019).

Read that carefully, because it describes your job. Building the structure is not the hard part. You have probably already built it. The structure only pays off if the founder actually uses it. That willingness is not something you can manufacture from your seat.

So the work splits in two. There is the operating design, which is yours to do. And there is the founder’s genuine handover of authority, which is theirs and which no amount of better process on your part will produce. Confusing the two is how capable people in your role spend three years getting tired.

The founder and the person running operations do not need to think alike. One may work through ideas in bursts, changing direction as new information arrives. The other needs a stable rhythm to turn those decisions into work the organisation can deliver. That difference can be useful. The trouble starts when the operating partner is held responsible for delivery but cannot make the decisions needed to deliver it.

#### What works from your seat

Ask for authority in writing and keep it narrow. Asking for more trust or more alignment gets you nothing measurable. Both quietly evaporate. Ask instead for a short list of named decisions you make without consulting anyone, agreed once and written down. This is the only reliable test of whether the structure is real. It is also the direct answer to the problem above.

Make the rhythm explicit instead of fighting it. Agree when decisions get made and when they may be reopened. A decision log with a closing date against each item does more than any volume of chasing, because it moves the argument from your memory to a shared document.

Take the formatting and leave the thinking. Stop asking your founder to write the pack. Get fifteen minutes of them talking, record it and write it yourself. You will get better material and it will arrive on time.

Put the consequential choices where the attention actually is. Most founders have two or three windows a week when their thinking is genuinely sharp. Protect those for decisions and stop defending a calendar nobody honours. The Spiky Profile is one way to see where those windows sit.

Name what you absorb, in operating language and without a diagnosis attached. Something like: I spend roughly half my week reconstructing decisions that were already made. Here is what I would do with that half instead. That sentence is about workflow. It is answerable. The personal version of the same sentence is not.

Make the absorbed work visible to the board. If nobody above you knows who holds the operating cadence, it will never be resourced and you will remain the single point of failure. Calling that politics misses the point: it is the only way the role survives your holiday.

Build a second absorber. If you are the only person who can translate, you are a risk to the company as well as to yourself.

#### If nothing moves

Some founders will not hand over authority. The research above suggests this is common rather than exceptional, which is worth knowing because it tells you that your failure to shift it is no reflection on your competence.

At that point you have three real options. It is better to choose one deliberately than to drift.

Shrink the role to what you can genuinely control. Stop being accountable for outcomes that depend on decisions you are not allowed to make. This is a smaller job. Sometimes it is also a sustainable one.

Take it to the board as a governance question rather than a personal one. Framed as operating risk and succession exposure, it is a legitimate thing for a board to hear. You are not being disloyal by raising it. Framed as a complaint about your founder, it will end badly for you.

Or leave, on your own timing, while you still have the energy to choose where you go next.

The option that does not work is continuing to absorb it silently in the hope that it resolves on its own. That ends in your departure anyway, later and in worse condition.

#### How solid any of this is

Worth saying plainly, because the field is often sold with more confidence than it has earned.

The evidence on how to design work around cognitive difference is considerably thinner than the evidence on medication. A systematic review from Birkbeck’s Centre for Neurodiversity Research at Work found that most intervention research in this area is pharmacological and that little is known about which workplace modifications actually improve outcomes (Lauder, McDowall and Tenenbaum, 2022).

The broader employment literature is more encouraging about direction than about method. A systematic review of 79 studies covering 68,275 adults with ADHD across 22 countries points consistently at the same three things: fit between the person and the role, autonomy in how the work gets done and a workplace where someone can turn to a colleague for help without a penalty (Hotte-Meunier et al., 2024).

Those are directions rather than protocols. The specifics above come from practice, including mine. They should be read as such.

#### One last thing

The variability you spend your week absorbing is usually attached to the capability that built the company. Those are two sides of the same person. A version of your founder who never reopened a decision would probably also be a version who never spotted the opening you are all now living off.

That does not mean you should carry the cost silently. The goal is a structure that holds the variance, rather than a founder who no longer has any.

#### Questions I get asked

#### My co-founder works in bursts and I cannot rely on him. What do I do?

Stop treating reliability as the measure and start separating the work. Identify which decisions genuinely need him and which are being routed through him out of habit. Then get a short written list of what you decide alone. Reliability across a week is the wrong unit for someone who works in cycles. Chasing it will exhaust you both. What you need is clarity about who owns what, which is achievable in an afternoon.

#### Should I tell my boss I think they have ADHD?

No. You could be wrong, it is not yours to name and it does not help you anyway. Raise the operating problem instead, in operating language: which decisions are getting reopened, what that costs in hours and what you propose doing about it. That conversation is yours to have and it needs no reference to anyone's health.

#### How do I support a CEO with ADHD without becoming their therapist?

By keeping the conversation on the work. You can own reporting, cadence, decision logs and the rhythm of the week. You cannot own their regulation, their recovery or their relationship with their own mind. Attempting it is how the role turns into something neither of you agreed to. If they need that kind of support, the right people are a coach and a clinician, not their chief of staff.

#### Is a chief of staff or a COO the right answer for a founder-led company?

Either can work. Neither works by itself. The evidence on founder-led firms suggests the surrounding team has little effect on operating performance unless the founder genuinely relies on it. So the question to settle before you hire is which decisions that person will make without asking and whether the founder will honour that when it is inconvenient. The title matters much less.

#### Am I being disloyal if I raise this with the board?

Not if you raise it as operating risk rather than as a complaint. Boards are entitled to understand where a company's execution capacity actually sits and what happens if one person goes on holiday. Framed that way it is a governance conversation and part of your job. Framed as a grievance about your founder, it will be heard as one.

References:
- Kofler, M. J., Rapport, M. D., Sarver, D. E., Raiker, J. S., Orban, S. A., Friedman, L. M. and Kolomeyer, E. G. (2013). Reaction time variability in ADHD: a meta-analytic review of 319 studies. Clinical Psychology Review, 33(6), 795 to 811.
- Tran, M. H., Wiklund, J., Antshel, K., Jhawar, N. and Montgomery, C. (2025). Entrepreneurship and ADHD: a meta-analytical assessment of the state of the art and suggestions for the future. Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice.
- Mylett, M., Iarocci, G. et al. (2026). Camouflaging in adults with ADHD. Research in Neurodiversity.
- Hendricks, B., Howell, T. and Bingham, C. (2019). How much do top management teams matter in founder-led firms? Strategic Management Journal, 40(6), 959 to 986.
- Lauder, K., McDowall, A. and Tenenbaum, H. R. (2022). A systematic review of interventions to support adults with ADHD at work: implications from the paucity of context-specific research for theory and practice. Frontiers in Psychology, 13. Centre for Neurodiversity Research at Work, Birkbeck, University of London.
- Hotte-Meunier, A., Sarraf, L., Bougeard, A. et al. (2024). Strengths and challenges to embrace attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in employment: a systematic review. Neurodiversity, 2.
